To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) BMI and waist circumference (WC) are independently and positively associated with all-cause and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality; 2) the association with BMI is stronger for all-cause mortality, whereas the association with WC is stronger for CVD mortality; 3) the association of BMI with mortality is stronger among men than among women, whereas the association of WC with mortality is not different between men and women; 4) the associations of both BMI and WC with mortality
a) waist circumference is associated with mortality in men and women, and b) waist circumference is a better predictor than BMI for mortality.
the association between BMI and mortality was similar in men and women, but that the association between WC and mortality was stronger in women.

a question that has been of considerable interest in the epidemiological and medical communities for many years: is there any evidence that a high waist circumference (WC), independent of body weight, is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality?

the question: what is the best way to predict mortality?

obesity is associated with an increased risk of mortality, but this association varies according to age, gender, and the measure of obesity.
the association between BMI and mortality is U-shaped, with an optimal level of BMI between 21 and 23 kg/m2, but with substantial variation in this association by age and sex.
the waist-to-hip ratio is a better indicator of mortality risk than the BMI, but that the BMI is a better indicator than the weight.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
waist circumference, but not BMI, is an important predictor of mortality in the elderly, and that the association is stronger than that for BMI.

waist circumference is a better predictor of mortality than body mass index.
